briefing.opening: Good day. We begin today's climate briefing for November 23, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 COP31 Ends Without Final Agreement for First Time in 17 Years Amid Fossil Fuel Conflicts
sections.content: The 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), held in Antalya, Türkiye, collapsed after failing to reach a final agreement for the first time in 17 years since 2009 [1, 12, 102, 112]. The breakdown occurred as clashes intensified between major oil-producing nations and climate-ambitious countries over explicit language regarding the phase-out of fossil fuels and climate finance mechanisms [8, 14, 70, 100]. The European Union (EU), the UK, and others firmly rejected any agreement that omitted a transition away from fossil fuels, bringing the longest-running conference in history to a close in deep division [12, 72, 106, 114, 124]. While UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that the science leaves no room for ambiguity, the presidency's closing gavel marked a major deadlock in international climate diplomacy [76, 81, 99].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Major Overhaul of South Korea's Renewable Energy Market: Phasing Out RPS and Transitioning to a Contract Market
sections.content: The South Korean government's climate ministry has unveiled a plan to phase out the existing Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS) and fully overhaul the system into a competitive bidding-based contract market [39, 43, 47, 55]. The competent ministry plans to hold a public briefing on the 27th to outline the detailed operational framework of the new contract market for power producers and industry stakeholders [47, 49]. This reform is being pursued to enhance electricity market efficiency and support a systematic expansion of renewable energy deployment [37, 43]. In connection with this, the International Energy Agency (IEA) analyzed that if South Korea successfully delivers on its deployment targets, including its 100 GW renewable energy goal, the country will be able to drastically reduce both its national energy import dependency and carbon emissions [36, 52].

sections.title: 🌱 Acceleration of Clean Energy Infrastructure at Home and Abroad: Solar-Driven Public-Private Partnerships Bear Fruit
sections.content: Despite difficulties in global multilateral negotiations, on-the-ground competition to implement renewable energy transitions is accelerating across industries [8, 64]. South Korea and Qatar agreed to significantly expand clean energy cooperation beyond traditional gas partnerships, highlighted by a 2 GW solar project involving Samsung C&T [46, 53, 65, 67]. Domestically, H Energy, GS Energy, and STIC have joined hands to combine power generation and financial capital to jointly develop 1 GW of rooftop solar power nationwide, with 60 MW slated to break ground within the year [50, 57, 61, 69]. Furthermore, corporate expansion into green business continues apace, marked by HMM signing eco-friendly 'Green Sailing' service agreements and LS Cable & System securing a 700 billion won power grid project in New York [38, 54].

sections.title: 🌍 Climate Impacts Hitting Daily Life as Grassroots Carbon-Neutral Practices Spread
sections.content: With global warming accelerating, the cultivation of subtropical crops such as mangoes and jicama is increasing in Jeju, rapidly altering South Korea's agricultural landscape [2]. In response to this crisis, community- and citizen-led climate action is also yielding tangible results [6, 17]. Through resident-led climate crisis initiatives, the proportion of farms practicing organic farming surged from 10% to 50%, while an emission reduction campaign driven by 3,416 youths cut 29 tons of greenhouse gas emissions [6, 17]. In addition, numerous best practices for carbon neutrality at the local government level have emerged, including Daejeon's Seo-gu receiving a ministerial award at a carbon neutrality contest and Seosan City winning an innovation grand prize for its resource recovery facility [18, 27].

briefing.closing: Even amid the uncertainty caused by the collapse of the international climate agreement, technological development, market reform, and grassroots action by civil society continue unabated. That concludes today's climate briefing.
